draft.title: Reactions of acids
card: Acid and metal
an acid reacts with a reactive metal to give a salt and hydrogen gas. Example: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen.
Acid and carbonate
an acid reacts with a carbonate to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Example: calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide.
Acid and base
an acid reacts with a base to give a salt and water. Example: sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water.

The salt's name comes from two parts. The first part is the metal or base's positive ion. The second part comes from the acid: chloride from hydrochloric acid, sulfate from sulfuric acid, nitrate from nitric acid.
draft.remember: Every acid reaction here makes a salt. The other products depend on whether the acid meets a metal, a carbonate or a base.

a.q: Which products form when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
opts: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
a.why: A carbonate contains carbon and oxygen, so the reaction gives off carbon dioxide along with a salt and water. A salt and water only is the result for a base, which has no carbonate to release gas.
a.clue: A carbonate reaction fizzes with a gas.

b.q: Zinc metal is added to dilute sulfuric acid. Which pair of products forms?
b.why: A metal and an acid give a salt and hydrogen gas. The salt takes zinc from the metal and sulfate from sulfuric acid, so it is zinc sulfate. Water is the product with a base, not a metal.
b.clue: Name the salt from the metal and the acid, then pick the gas.

a.best: A salt, water and carbon dioxide

problems.detail: The salt-naming rule says the first part is 'the metal or base's positive ion', but it leaves out carbonates, even though the card's own example gets calcium from calcium carbonate. Saying 'the positive ion from the metal, carbonate or base' would match all three reactions.

check.summary: Both questions and explanations are correct. The only issue is that the salt-naming line on the card mentions metals and bases but leaves out carbonates, which its own calcium carbonate example uses.
